objectAssessments.assessment: Preserves particle motion/interactions and qualitative explanations of phases and thermal phenomena. The added qualitative definition usefully separates explanation from numerical prediction.

Why versus how much makes the qualitative/quantitative distinction accessible. Statistical mechanics is introduced through distributions and averages rather than as a substitute for individual mechanics; gas focus is retained.
Newtonian mechanics is not generalized without conditions to all microscopic phenomena. The quantum qualification is appropriate without inventing a temperature, density, size or speed threshold.
Classical particle motion/collisions are conditional model assumptions. Experimental agreement supports the model in applicable tested conditions, not proof of universal atomic validity.
Motion, interactions and distributions are connected to macroscopic properties. The speed-distribution explanation is useful and does not confuse average motion with every particle having one speed.

Molecular impacts transfer momentum and exert wall force. Average force perpendicular to the wall divided by receiving area is dimensionally and physically appropriate pressure, not single-particle force or tangential stress. Finite area/time and instrument response averaging are distinguished; stability is qualified to macroscopic equilibrium and small relative fluctuations, not no fluctuations. Figure 45 is expressly qualitative, not a measured dataset. The added momentum sentence is not a useful identifying definition, and the figure disclaimer crosses a display-paragraph boundary within one sentence.
Figure 45 object, position and source identity retained with no text or asset mutation. This is reference fidelity only, not new pixel approval.
Figure 45 caption is correctly translated; the internal source label is retained and no calibration or values are added.

findings.excerpt: Momentum is the mechanical quantity transferred in a collision that changes a body's motion.
findings.assessment: This describes a use of momentum, not what the quantity is. A learner cannot distinguish it from other transferred mechanical quantities or connect it to the classical particle motion used in the pressure explanation.
findings.action: Replace the gloss with a concise classical definition in words, such as momentum being a particle's mass times its velocity, with the velocity's direction. Retain the surrounding collision-to-wall-force explanation. No new numerical data, equation, task, source change or figure change is needed.
findings.acceptance: The revised saved English paragraph identifies momentum by mass and velocity rather than only by its transfer role, while preserving the qualified classical setting and the later normal-force-per-area definition.
